To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the addition of background sound modulates both subcortically and cortically evoked responses, and that relationships between neural measures and behavioral measures emerge only with the addition background noise.

subcortical brainstem responses and cortical N1 response amplitude reflect coordinated processing with regards to the perceptual ability of normal hearing young adults to discriminate speech in noise.

subcortical neural responses are delayed by noise and that the amplitude of the major peaks of cortical evoked responses (the N1 and P2) are affected differently by noise, with N1 amplitude increasing and P2 amplitude decreasing, and the amplitude of the N1 peak of cortical evoked response is related to better speech in noise perception.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the biological basis of the ability to perceive speech in the presence of background noise.
the neural processing of speech in the context of background noise and how this processing may be related to speech perception.
the neural basis of the perception of speech‐in noise, and how the brain responds to the acoustic signal of speech.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
subcortical neural processing and cortical processing of speech in noise is a complex and coordinated process.

the brainstem and N1 responses reflect a functional index of the perception of speech‐in noise, and that the neural encoding of speech‐in-noise processing is reflected in the morphology of both subcortically‐ and cortically‐evoked responses.

the subcortical brainstem and the N1 cortical response are both sensitive to the presence of background noise, and both reflect coordinated processes in relation to the perception of the speech signal in noise.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the neural processing of speech sounds in noise is reflected in the amplitude of the brainstem response, and the morphology of the N1 component of the auditory cortex.

speech‐in‐noiseprocessing is supported by the coordinated activity of both subcortically‐ and cortically‐generated responses, with the neural encoding of speech sounds in the auditory brainstem and the N1 cortical response reflecting the ability to process speech in the presence of competing background noise.

the neural encoding of speech in noise is a coordinated process, and that both subcortically and cortically generated responses are sensitive to the acoustic properties of the background noise and the speech signal.
The main takeaway from our work is that
speech‐in‐‐noise perception can be indexed by both subcortically and cortically evoked responses, with the latter providing a better index of speech‐ in‐noise perception.
subcortical processing is a critical component in speech perception in noise.
the subcortical brainstem and cortical N1 response can be used to predict the behavioral measure of speech in noise in young adults.
